name: Carian
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Adiego, I. J. 2007. The Carian Language (Handbook of Oriental Studies). Brill.
earlier_scan.note: Ancient Anatolian language in an alphabetic script; Adiego's phonology chapter is the only plausible venue, accent likely unrecoverable.

new_statements.quote: In the first group with one vowel, since a single vowel was always preserved, the most straightforward assumption is that this vowel is the accented one. In other words, the vowel accented in Carian pronunciation was kept and all other vowels were dropped. [...] All in all, we can establish the rule that Carian preserved the accented vowel (in this case in its Egyptian place) and deleted all other vowels, except the [i] of a following (post-tonic) syllable. [...] From the point of view of Carian synchronic phonology, the proposed rule generally explains the “vowellessness” of the Carian words and further supports Adiego’s analysis (2019) that the written form should be taken seriously phonologically
new_statements.citation: Simon, Zsolt. 2023. "Egyptian in Carian transmission: Towards a better understanding of Carian vocalism." In J. V. Garcia Trabazo et al. (eds.), New approaches on Anatolian linguistics (Barcino Monographica Orientalia 22, Series Anatolica et Indogermanica 4), 241-252. Barcelona: Edicions de la Universitat de Barcelona.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Files checked in ( present and accurate). (1) Simon 2023 in /.txt: all three quoted fragments are present verbatim at the stated locators. PDF page numbering coincides with printed pagination (article starts PDF p. 241). Fragment 1 'In the first group with one vowel, since a single vowel was always preserved, the most straightforward assumption is that this vowel is the accented one. In other words, the vowel accented in Carian pronunciation was kept and all other vowels were dropped.' = sec. 3, p. 246 (txt lines 9733-9737); fragment 2 'All in all, we can establish the rule that Carian preserved the accented vowel (in this case in its Egyptian place) and deleted all other vowels, except the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Carian had a strong dynamic (stress) accent: only the accented vowel of a word survives/is written, unaccented vowels are reduced or deleted (a post-tonic [i] may remain). The position of the accent is not fixed by any stated rule: in loans it stays where the source language had it, and in native words it is recoverable only per word from which vowel is written; Adiego 2019: 24 adds that pretonic syllables were weakened and tonic syllables lengthened, with the accent moving onto suffixes (*knda(acute)wa- 'king' vs. *kndawa-sa(acute) 'kingship' > kδuso). No source opened gives a positional (initial/penult/etc.) rule; the reading 'lexical' is an inference from these statements, not an explicit claim of the sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Post-tonic [i] (from Egyptian schwa) may be kept (ntokris, ptnupi, ttbazi); apmen keeps a pretonic a- as an anaptyctic vowel because initial pm- was not permitted; artmon (Greek Artemon) apparently contradicts the rule but may be a local name form; pismaśk shows secondary epenthetic i.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent inferred from spellings of personal names and loanwords (Caromemphite corpus, 7th-5th c. BC) and from Greek renderings; Carian script does not mark accent, so all statements are reconstructive. Simon's rule is synchronic loan adaptation which he extends to native 'vowelless' spellings; Hajnal 1995:17-21 proposed the same as a historical rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Carian (xcr, cari1274), an alphabetically written Anatolian corpus language (7th-3rd c. BC); the accent evidence comes chiefly from the Caromemphite (Carian-of-Egypt: Saqqara/Memphis) sub-corpus and from Greek renderings of Carian names, not from a living variety. No dialect split relevant to glottocodes.

sources.note: pp. 246-249: from Egyptian (and Greek) names/loans written in Carian, formulates the rule that Carian kept only the accented vowel and dropped/left unwritten all unaccented vowels (except a post-tonic [i]); accent placement in loans follows the source language; says this rule 'generally explains the vowellessness of the Carian words'; notes Hajnal 1995:17-21 already proposed historically that only accented vowels were preserved. No positional rule for native word accent.

sources.citation: Adiego, Ignasi-Xavier. 2019. "A Kingdom for a Carian Letter." In I.-X. Adiego et al. (eds.), Luwic Dialects and Anatolian: Inheritance and Diffusion (Barcino Monographica Orientalia 12), 11-50. Barcelona: Edicions UB.
sources.note: p. 24 (sec. 8.2): 'It seems that in Carian there was a tendency to weaken pretonic syllables, together with a tendency to lengthen tonic syllables (and, in the case of a-macron-acute, to round in o). Thus *knda(acute)wa- > /kndow-/, but *kndawa+sa(acute) > /kndusow-/. A comparable phenomenon can be detected in kbid- vs. kbdyns... and perhaps also in the personal name Usseldomos/Ussaldomos vs. usol... */usa(acute)lla-/ > /usol/, but */usalla(acute)ma-/ > */us@lom-/.' I.e. accent position reconstructed per word/etymologically, shifting rightward under suffixation; no general placement rule.

sources.note: IV.1.1 Fonetica, sec. 4 'Ausencia de vocales' (pp. 610-611): consonant clusters/unwritten vowels may be graphic or phonetic: 'en cario existirian vocales reducidas (quizas por efecto de algun tipo de acento intensivo) no recogidas graficamente'; plus syllabic sonorants.
